title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions
overview: Polynomial functions model profit, volume, population and motion. In this section you learn to read a polynomial's 'personality' straight from its equation: the **degree** and the **sign of the leading coefficient** tell you the end behaviour, how many times the graph can cross the $x$-axis, how many hills and valleys it can have, and whether it has a highest or lowest point. You will also use **finite differences** to recognise a polynomial from a table of values.
objectives: Identify polynomial functions and state their degree and leading coefficient.
Describe end behaviour using the degree and the sign of the leading coefficient.
Relate the degree to the possible number of $x$-intercepts and turning points.
Distinguish local and absolute maximum and minimum points.
Use finite differences to find the degree and leading coefficient from a table.
Interpret polynomial models and choose a reasonable domain.

lessons.title: What makes a function a polynomial?
lessons.body:
A **polynomial function** has the form

$$f(x) = a_nx^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_2x^2 + a_1x + a_0$$

where every exponent is a **whole number** ($0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$) and the coefficients $a_n, a_{n-1}, \dots, a_0$ are real numbers.

| Vocabulary | Meaning | In $f(x) = -3x^4 + 2x^2 - x + 7$ |
|---|---|---|
| **degree** | the highest exponent, $n$ | $4$ (a *quartic*) |
| **leading coefficient** | the coefficient $a_n$ of the highest-power term | $-3$ |
| **constant term** | $a_0$, which is also the $y$-intercept | $7$ |

A **power function** such as $y = x^3$ or $y = -2x^4$ is the simplest polynomial: just one term. Every polynomial graph "inherits" its long-run shape from its leading term, because for very large $|x|$ the highest power dominates everything else.

**Not polynomials:** $y = x^{-2}$ (negative exponent), $y = \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ (fractional exponent), $y = 3^x$ (the variable is in the exponent), $y = \dfrac{1}{x+1}$.

> **Tip:** expand or think about the product before deciding. $g(x) = x(4 - x) = -x^2 + 4x$ is a quadratic with leading coefficient $-1$.

| Degree | Name |
|---|---|
| 0 | constant |
| 1 | linear |
| 2 | quadratic |
| 3 | cubic |
| 4 | quartic |
| 5 | quintic |

lessons.title: End behaviour: degree and the sign of the leading coefficient
lessons.body:
**End behaviour** describes what $y$ does as $x \to \infty$ (far right) and as $x \to -\infty$ (far left). Only two things matter: whether the degree is **odd or even**, and whether the leading coefficient is **positive or negative**.

| | Leading coefficient $> 0$ | Leading coefficient $< 0$ |
|---|---|---|
| **Odd degree** | quadrant 3 → quadrant 1 (like $y = x$): as $x\to-\infty$, $y\to-\infty$; as $x\to\infty$, $y\to\infty$ | quadrant 2 → quadrant 4 (like $y = -x$) |
| **Even degree** | quadrant 2 → quadrant 1 (like $y = x^2$): both ends up | quadrant 3 → quadrant 4 (like $y = -x^2$): both ends down |

Odd-degree graphs have ends pointing in **opposite** directions; even-degree graphs have ends pointing in the **same** direction.

```plot
title: Odd degree, positive (blue) vs even degree, positive (red)
f: x^3 - 4*x | label=y = x³ − 4x (odd)
f: x^4 - 5*x^2 + 4 | label=y = x⁴ − 5x² + 4 (even)
domain: -3, 3
range: -8, 8
```

**Domain and range**
* Every polynomial has domain $\{x \in \mathbb{R}\}$.
* An **odd**-degree polynomial has range $\{y \in \mathbb{R}\}$: it eventually goes up forever on one side and down forever on the other.
* An **even**-degree polynomial with $a_n > 0$ has a lowest point, so its range is $\{y \in \mathbb{R},\ y \ge a\}$ where $a$ is the minimum value. With $a_n < 0$ the range is $\{y \in \mathbb{R},\ y \le a\}$ where $a$ is the maximum value.

lessons.title: Turning points and x-intercepts
lessons.body:
A **local maximum** is a point that is higher than all nearby points (a "hilltop"); a **local minimum** is lower than all nearby points (a "valley"). An **absolute** (global) maximum or minimum is the highest or lowest point on the *whole* graph.

For a polynomial of degree $n$:

| Feature | Odd degree $n$ | Even degree $n$ |
|---|---|---|
| number of $x$-intercepts | at least 1, at most $n$ | from 0 up to $n$ |
| local max + local min (turning points) | at most $n - 1$ (an even number) | at most $n - 1$ (an odd number, at least 1) |
| absolute max / min | none | exactly one kind: a minimum if $a_n>0$, a maximum if $a_n<0$ |

**Why must an odd-degree graph cross the $x$-axis?** Its ends go in opposite directions — one end below the axis, the other above. A polynomial graph is one unbroken curve, so it has to cross the $x$-axis somewhere in between.

**Reading a graph backwards:** if a graph has 3 turning points, its degree is **at least 4** (because $n - 1 \ge 3$). If its ends go in opposite directions, the degree is odd.

```plot
title: Quartic: 3 turning points, 4 x-intercepts
f: -0.25*(x+3)*(x+1)*(x-2)*(x-3)
domain: -4, 4
range: -6, 8
points: (-3,0), (-1,0), (2,0), (3,0)
```

The quartic above has a negative leading coefficient (both ends down), two local maxima and one local minimum — a total of $3 = 4 - 1$ turning points. Its highest hilltop is also the absolute maximum.

lessons.title: Finite differences
lessons.body:
When $x$-values in a table go up in **equal steps**, we can subtract consecutive $y$-values to get **first differences**, then subtract those to get **second differences**, and so on.

For a polynomial function of degree $n$, the $n$th differences

* are **constant** (all equal),
* have the **same sign** as the leading coefficient $a$, and
* equal $a \times n!$ when the $x$-step is 1, where $n! = n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 2 \times 1$.

| Degree $n$ | constant difference | so $a =$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $a \times 1$ | first difference ÷ 1 |
| 2 | $a \times 2$ | second difference ÷ 2 |
| 3 | $a \times 6$ | third difference ÷ 6 |
| 4 | $a \times 24$ | fourth difference ÷ 24 |
| 5 | $a \times 120$ | fifth difference ÷ 120 |

**Example.** $y = x^3 - x^2$ for $x = -3, -2, \dots, 4$:

| $x$ | $y$ | 1st | 2nd | 3rd |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| −3 | −36 | | | |
| −2 | −12 | 24 | | |
| −1 | −2 | 10 | −14 | |
| 0 | 0 | 2 | −8 | 6 |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | −2 | 6 |
| 2 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 6 |
| 3 | 18 | 14 | 10 | 6 |
| 4 | 48 | 30 | 16 | 6 |

The third differences are constant, so the function is **cubic**. They are positive, so $a > 0$, and $6 = a \times 3! = 6a$ gives $a = 1$.

> Always subtract in the same order: **later value minus earlier value**.

lessons.title: Polynomial models in the real world
lessons.body:
Many quantities that rise and fall are modelled by polynomials: profit, the volume of a box, the height of a falling object, a bacteria population.

**Bacteria example.** After an antibacterial spray is applied, a culture's population is

| $t$ (min) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P$ | 800 | 799 | 782 | 737 | 652 | 515 | 314 | 37 |

The third differences are all $-12$, so the model is cubic with $-12 = 6a$, giving $a = -2$. Regression on a graphing calculator gives $P(t) = -2t^3 - 2t^2 + 3t + 800$.

**Reasonable domain.** A model is only meaningful where the situation makes sense. Here $t \ge 0$ (time starts when the spray is applied) and $P \ge 0$ (no negative bacteria), so roughly $0 \le t \le 7.1$ minutes. Outside that interval the equation still produces numbers, but they describe nothing real.

**Questions to ask about any model**
1. What do the degree and leading coefficient say about long-run behaviour — and does that match reality?
2. What restrictions on the domain are reasonable?
3. What do the intercepts mean in context?

keyTerms.definition: A function of the form $f(x)=a_nx^n+\dots+a_1x+a_0$ where $n$ is a whole number and the coefficients are real numbers.
The highest exponent of $x$ in a polynomial function.
The coefficient of the term with the highest power of $x$.
The behaviour of $y$ as $x\to\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$, often described with quadrants (e.g. 'from quadrant 3 to quadrant 1').
A point that is higher (or lower) than all points near it; also called a turning point.
The highest (or lowest) point on the entire graph. Only even-degree polynomials have one.
Differences between consecutive $y$-values in a table whose $x$-values are equally spaced.

formulas.name: General polynomial
formulas.meaning: $n$ is the degree and $a_n$ the leading coefficient.

formulas.name: Constant finite differences
formulas.meaning: For $x$-steps of 1, the $n$th differences of a degree-$n$ polynomial equal the leading coefficient times $n!$.

formulas.name: Maximum number of turning points
formulas.meaning: A degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n-1$ local maximum and minimum points.

workedExamples.title: Describe a polynomial from its equation
workedExamples.problem: For $g(x) = -x^4 + 10x^2 + 5x - 4$, state the degree, leading coefficient, end behaviour, $y$-intercept, possible number of $x$-intercepts and the maximum number of turning points.
steps: **Degree and leading coefficient.** The highest power is $x^4$, so the degree is 4 (quartic) and the leading coefficient is $-1$.
**End behaviour.** Even degree with a negative leading coefficient: both ends point down, so the graph extends from quadrant 3 to quadrant 4.
**y-intercept.** Set $x = 0$: $g(0) = -4$.
**x-intercepts.** An even-degree polynomial can have 0 to 4 $x$-intercepts. (A graph shows this one has 4.)
**Turning points.** At most $4 - 1 = 3$. With a negative leading coefficient it has an absolute maximum and no absolute minimum.
workedExamples.answer: Quartic, $a=-1$, Q3 → Q4, $y$-intercept $-4$, 0–4 $x$-intercepts, at most 3 turning points.

workedExamples.title: Degree and leading coefficient from a table
steps: Second differences: $-38, -2, 10, -2, -38, -98$.
Third differences: $36, 12, -12, -36, -60$.
Fourth differences: $-24, -24, -24, -24$ — constant, so the function is **quartic** (degree 4).
The constant difference is negative, so $a<0$. Solve $-24 = a \times 4! = 24a$, so $a = -1$.

workedExamples.title: From a constant difference to the leading coefficient
workedExamples.problem: The fifth differences of a polynomial function (with $x$-steps of 1) are constant at $-60$. State the degree and the leading coefficient.
steps: Fifth differences are constant, so the degree is 5.

workedExamples.title: A falling parachutist
workedExamples.problem: A parachutist jumps from 3500 m. Their height is $h(t) = 3500 - 4.9t^2$. Without building a table, which differences are constant and what is their value? What is a reasonable domain?
steps: $h$ is quadratic (degree 2), so the **second** differences are constant.
Their value is $a \times 2! = -4.9 \times 2 = -9.8$.
End behaviour of the equation: both ends down (Q3 → Q4). In reality the model only applies while the parachutist is in the air.
Set $h = 0$: $t^2 = \dfrac{3500}{4.9} \approx 714.3$, so $t \approx 26.7$ s. A reasonable domain is $0 \le t \le 26.7$ (ignoring the parachute opening).
workedExamples.answer: Second differences, constant at −9.8; domain about $0 \le t \le 26.7$ s.

workedExamples.title: Box volume model
workedExamples.problem: Squares of side $x$ cm are cut from the corners of a 30 cm by 20 cm sheet, and the sides are folded up to make an open box. Write the volume function and describe its degree, leading coefficient and reasonable domain.
steps: Length $30 - 2x$, width $20 - 2x$, height $x$: $V(x) = x(30 - 2x)(20 - 2x)$.
Multiplying the $x$-terms: $x \cdot (-2x)\cdot(-2x) = 4x^3$, so it is cubic with leading coefficient 4.
All three dimensions must be positive: $x > 0$ and $20 - 2x > 0 \Rightarrow x < 10$.
Reasonable domain: $0 < x < 10$. Outside this, the equation gives values but no real box exists.

misconceptions.myth: The degree tells you exactly how many $x$-intercepts there are.
misconceptions.fact: The degree is only the *maximum*. A quartic can have 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 $x$-intercepts.

misconceptions.myth: The leading coefficient is the first number written in the equation.
misconceptions.fact: It is the coefficient of the **highest power**. In $f(x) = 5 + 2x - 3x^3$ the leading coefficient is $-3$.

misconceptions.myth: A cubic always has two turning points.
misconceptions.fact: A cubic has either 0 or 2 turning points ($y = x^3$ has none). It can never have exactly 1.

misconceptions.myth: Second differences are always the ones to check.
misconceptions.fact: Keep taking differences until they are constant; the step at which they become constant gives the degree.

misconceptions.myth: A local maximum is the highest point on the graph.
misconceptions.fact: A local maximum is only the highest point *nearby*. An odd-degree polynomial has local maxima but no absolute maximum.

realWorld.title: Medicine
realWorld.body: Reaction time after a dose of a drug can be modelled by a polynomial such as $r(d) = -0.7d^3 + d^2$, valid only for small doses.

realWorld.title: Packaging design
realWorld.body: The volume of an open box folded from a sheet is cubic; designers use the model to choose the cut size that gives the most volume.

realWorld.title: Biology
realWorld.body: Finite differences in lab data reveal whether a population model should be quadratic, cubic or higher before running a regression.

realWorld.title: Physics
realWorld.body: Height of a falling object, $h(t) = h_0 - 4.9t^2$, is quadratic: its second differences are constant at $-9.8$ for 1-s steps.

practice.question: State the degree, leading coefficient and end behaviour of $f(x) = 2x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 1$.
practice.solution: Degree 3, leading coefficient 2. As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to-\infty$; as $x\to\infty$, $y\to\infty$ (quadrant 3 to quadrant 1).

practice.question: Is $h(x) = 3^x + 2x$ a polynomial function? Explain.
practice.solution: No. In $3^x$ the variable is an exponent, so it is an exponential term, not a power of $x$ with a whole-number exponent.

practice.question: What is the maximum number of turning points of a degree-6 polynomial? The minimum number of $x$-intercepts?
practice.hint: Use $n-1$, and remember even-degree graphs may not cross the axis.
practice.solution: At most $6-1 = 5$ turning points. The minimum number of $x$-intercepts is 0 (for example $y = x^6 + 1$).

practice.question: The third differences of a polynomial are constant at 42. Find the degree and leading coefficient.
Explain why $y = -2x^5 + 5x^3 - x$ has no maximum point and no minimum point.
practice.solution: It has odd degree with a negative leading coefficient, so as $x\to-\infty$, $y\to\infty$ and as $x\to\infty$, $y\to-\infty$. The graph rises and falls without bound, so there is no highest or lowest point (only local ones).

practice.question: Write the range of $f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2 + 3$ if its minimum value is $-13$.
The table $x = 0,1,2,3,4$; $y = 5, 7, 13, 23, 37$ comes from a polynomial. Find its degree and leading coefficient.
practice.solution: First differences 2, 6, 10, 14; second differences 4, 4, 4. Quadratic, and $4 = 2a$ so $a = 2$.

practice.question: Sketch-describe a polynomial with degree 5, positive leading coefficient and exactly 3 $x$-intercepts.
practice.hint: Some intercepts can be touch points.
practice.solution: Example: $y = (x+2)(x-1)(x-3)(x^2+1)$. Multiplying the $x$-terms gives $x^5$, so the degree is 5 and $a = 1 > 0$. The factor $x^2 + 1$ is never 0, so the only $x$-intercepts are $-2, 1, 3$. The graph runs from quadrant 3 to quadrant 1, crossing the axis at each intercept.

summary: A polynomial has whole-number exponents; its degree is the highest exponent and its leading coefficient multiplies that term.
Odd degree: ends in opposite directions, range all real numbers, at least one $x$-intercept, no absolute max or min.
Even degree: ends in the same direction, has an absolute minimum ($a>0$) or maximum ($a<0$), from 0 to $n$ $x$-intercepts.
A degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n-1$ turning points and at most $n$ $x$-intercepts.
The $n$th finite differences of a degree-$n$ polynomial are constant, have the sign of $a$, and equal $a\times n!$ (for $x$-steps of 1).

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The highest power is $x^5$, so the degree is **5**.

(b) The leading coefficient is $-{{a}}$.

(c) Odd degree and negative leading coefficient: as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to \infty$ and as $x \to \infty$, $y \to -\infty$. The graph extends from **quadrant 2 to quadrant 4**.

(d) An odd-degree polynomial has at least 1 and at most 5 $x$-intercepts, and at most $5 - 1 = 4$ turning points.

(e) The $y$-intercept is $f(0) = -7$.

questions.text: A polynomial function has degree $n = {{n}}$. Answer each part and justify your reasoning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the greatest possible number of $x$-intercepts?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the greatest possible number of turning points?

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the least possible number of $x$-intercepts? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A degree-$n$ polynomial can cross or touch the $x$-axis at most $n$ times: at most **{{n}}** $x$-intercepts.

(b) The number of turning points is at most $n - 1 = {{n-1}}$.

(c) If $n$ is odd the ends point in opposite directions, so the graph must cross the $x$-axis at least once (minimum 1). If $n$ is even both ends point the same way, so the graph can stay entirely above or below the axis (minimum 0). For $n = {{n}}$ the minimum is **{{n - 2*floor(n/2)}}**.

rubric.point: Justifies minimum using end behaviour (odd vs even)

questions.text: The fourth differences of a polynomial function (with $x$-values increasing by 1) are constant and equal to {{-24*a}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the degree.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of the leading coefficient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the leading coefficient.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the end behaviour and state whether the graph has a maximum or minimum point.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Fourth differences are constant, so the degree is **4** (quartic).

(b) The leading coefficient has the same sign as the constant differences, so it is **negative**.

(c) $-{{24*a}} = a_4 \times 4! = 24a_4$, so $a_4 = -{{a}}$.

(d) An even-degree polynomial with a negative leading coefficient extends from quadrant 3 to quadrant 4 and has an **absolute maximum** point but no minimum point.

rubric.point: End behaviour and maximum point described

questions.text: Explain, using end behaviour, why every polynomial function of odd degree has at least one $x$-intercept, while a polynomial function of even degree may have none. Give an example of an even-degree function with no $x$-intercepts.
questions.modelAnswer:
An odd-degree polynomial has ends pointing in **opposite** directions: if $a > 0$, $y \to -\infty$ on the left and $y \to \infty$ on the right (reversed if $a<0$). Since a polynomial graph is a single unbroken (continuous) curve, it must pass from below the $x$-axis to above it, so it crosses the axis at least once.

An even-degree polynomial has both ends pointing in the **same** direction (both up if $a>0$). The whole graph can therefore stay above (or below) the $x$-axis. Example: $f(x) = x^4 + 3$ has minimum value 3, so it never reaches the $x$-axis.

rubric.point: Odd degree: ends in opposite directions
Uses continuity / unbroken curve to argue a crossing
Even degree: ends in same direction so can avoid axis

questions.text: A parachutist jumps from a plane {{H}} m above the ground. Their height, in metres, $t$ seconds after the jump is modelled by $h(t) = {{H}} - 4.9t^2$ (ignore the parachute).

parts.label: a
parts.text: What type of function is $h(t)$?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Without making a table, state which finite differences are constant and their value. Explain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the end behaviour if the domain is not restricted.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine a reasonable domain and explain what the positive $t$-intercept represents.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $h(t)$ is a **quadratic** (degree 2) function.

(b) For a degree-2 polynomial the **second** differences are constant. Their value is $a \times 2! = -4.9 \times 2 = -9.8$ (for 1-second steps).

(c) As an equation with no restrictions, both ends point down: as $t \to \pm\infty$, $h \to -\infty$ (quadrant 3 to quadrant 4).

(d) Set $h(t) = 0$: $4.9t^2 = {{H}}$, so $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{ {{H}} }{4.9}} \approx {{sqrt(H/4.9):3}}$ s. A reasonable domain is $0 \le t \le {{sqrt(H/4.9):3}}$, since time starts at the jump and the model ends at the ground. The positive $t$-intercept is the time the parachutist would reach the ground.

rubric.point: Reasonable domain and meaning of t-intercept

questions.text:
The graph of a polynomial function is shown.

```plot
f: -0.25*(x+3)*(x+1)*(x-2)*(x-3)
domain: -4, 4
range: -8, 10
points: (-3,0), (-1,0), (2,0), (3,0)
```

parts.label: a
parts.text: Is the degree odd or even? Is the leading coefficient positive or negative? Explain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the least possible degree. Justify.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the $x$-intercepts.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe any maximum or minimum points and the form of the range.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Both ends point down (quadrant 3 to quadrant 4), so the degree is **even** and the leading coefficient is **negative**.

(b) The graph has 3 turning points (two local maxima and one local minimum). Since a degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n-1$ turning points, $n - 1 \ge 3$, so the least possible degree is **4**.

(c) There are 4 $x$-intercepts: $-3, -1, 2, 3$.

(d) It has an absolute maximum (the higher of the two hilltops) and no absolute minimum. Range: $\{y\in\mathbb{R},\ y \le M\}$ where $M$ is that maximum value.

rubric.point: Least possible degree 4 using turning points
Absolute maximum, no minimum, range form

questions.text: Create an equation for a polynomial function that has degree 5, a negative leading coefficient, a $y$-intercept of {{k}}, and exactly three distinct $x$-intercepts. Explain how your equation meets each condition and describe the end behaviour.
questions.modelAnswer:
One possible answer: $f(x) = -\dfrac{ {{k}} }{6}(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)(x^2 + 1)$.

Check the $y$-intercept: $f(0) = -\dfrac{ {{k}} }{6}(-1)(-2)(-3)(1) = -\dfrac{ {{k}} }{6}(-6) = {{k}}$ ✓

* Degree: the factors contain $x \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x^2 = x^5$ ✓
* Leading coefficient: $-\dfrac{ {{k}} }{6} < 0$ ✓
* $x$-intercepts: $1, 2, 3$ only, because $x^2 + 1 = 0$ has no real solutions ✓ (another approach: use a repeated factor such as $(x-1)^2(x-2)^2(x-3)$ times a negative constant.)
* End behaviour: odd degree, negative leading coefficient → quadrant 2 to quadrant 4.

Any equation that satisfies all four conditions with a correct explanation earns full marks.

rubric.point: y-intercept equals the required value (shown by substitution)

questions.text: Determine the value of the constant finite differences for $f(x) = {{a}}x^4 - 3x^2 + x$ (using $x$-values that increase by 1), and state which differences they are.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which differences are constant?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine their value.

questions.modelAnswer:
The degree is 4, so the **fourth** differences are constant.

Value $= a \times 4! = {{a}} \times 24 = {{24*a}}$.

The other terms ($-3x^2 + x$) do not affect the fourth differences.

questions.text: A student examines a table of values with $x$-values $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and finds that the second differences are all equal to {{2*a}}. The student concludes: "The leading coefficient is {{2*a}}." Explain the error and give the correct leading coefficient. Then describe the graph's end behaviour and range type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Correct leading coefficient

questions.modelAnswer:
The student forgot that the constant $n$th differences equal $a \times n!$, not $a$. Here $n = 2$ (second differences constant), so

$${{2*a}} = a \times 2! = 2a \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = {{a}}.$$

The function is quadratic with a positive leading coefficient, so it opens up: both ends rise (quadrant 2 to quadrant 1). It has a minimum value, so the range has the form $\{y \in \mathbb{R},\ y \ge k\}$ where $k$ is the minimum.

rubric.point: Identifies that differences equal a × n!
Range has a minimum value form

questions.text: Explain why the graph of a cubic function can have zero or two turning points but never exactly one. Use sketches described in words, or the example $y = x^3$ and $y = x^3 - 3x$.
questions.modelAnswer:
A cubic with $a > 0$ falls to $-\infty$ on the left and rises to $\infty$ on the right. If the graph turned exactly once, it would change from rising to falling (or falling to rising) and then keep going that way forever — but then the right-hand end could not rise. To end up going up, every "turn down" must be followed by a "turn up". So turning points come in pairs: 0 or 2 for a cubic (at most $3 - 1 = 2$).

* $y = x^3$ rises all the time: 0 turning points.
* $y = x^3 - 3x$ rises, turns down at a local maximum $(-1, 2)$, then turns back up at a local minimum $(1, -2)$: 2 turning points.

rubric.point: Argues turns must come in pairs to match the ends

questions.text: An open-top box is made from a {{L}} cm by {{W}} cm sheet of cardboard by cutting squares of side $x$ cm from each corner and folding up the sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the volume, $V(x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the degree and the leading coefficient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a reasonable domain. Explain.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the end behaviour of the unrestricted function and why most of it has no meaning here.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $V(x) = x({{L}} - 2x)({{W}} - 2x)$.

(b) Multiplying the $x$-terms of each factor gives $x(-2x)(-2x) = 4x^3$: the function is **cubic** with leading coefficient **4**.

(c) Every dimension must be positive: $x > 0$, ${{W}} - 2x > 0 \Rightarrow x < {{W/2}}$ (and ${{L}} - 2x > 0 \Rightarrow x < {{L/2}}$). So the reasonable domain is $0 < x < {{W/2}}$.

(d) Without restrictions, a cubic with a positive leading coefficient goes from quadrant 3 to quadrant 1. Outside $0 < x < {{W/2}}$ the values (including positive values for $x > {{L/2}}$) do not represent a real box.

rubric.point: Comments on end behaviour vs reality

questions.text:
For each function, decide whether it is a polynomial function. If it is, state its degree and leading coefficient; if not, explain why not.

$f(x) = 3x^4 - 5x + 1$, $\quad g(x) = x(4 - x)$, $\quad h(x) = 3^x + 2x$, $\quad m(x) = x^{-2}$, $\quad r(x) = 5(x - 1)^3$
questions.modelAnswer:
* $f$: polynomial, degree 4, leading coefficient 3.
* $g(x) = x(4-x) = -x^2 + 4x$: polynomial, degree 2, leading coefficient $-1$.
* $h$: **not** a polynomial — $3^x$ has the variable in the exponent.
* $m$: **not** a polynomial — the exponent $-2$ is not a whole number.
* $r(x) = 5(x-1)^3$: polynomial, degree 3; expanding, the $x^3$ term is $5x^3$, so the leading coefficient is 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the end behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the minimum value of the function. Explain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the domain and range.

parts.label: d
parts.text: How many $x$-intercepts does the graph have? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Expanding, $(x^2)^2 = x^4$, so the leading coefficient is **1** (positive) and the degree is 4. Both ends point up: quadrant 2 to quadrant 1.

(b) $(x^2 - {{p}})^2 \ge 0$ for all $x$, and it equals 0 when $x^2 = {{p}}$, i.e. $x = \pm\sqrt{ {{p}} }$. So the minimum value of $f$ is **{{k}}**.

(c) Range: $\{y \in \mathbb{R},\ y \ge {{k}}\}$. Domain: $\{x \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

(d) Since the minimum value {{k}} is positive, the graph never reaches the $x$-axis: **0** $x$-intercepts — which shows an even-degree polynomial can have no $x$-intercepts.

rubric.point: Degree, leading coefficient and end behaviour
Explains square is never negative to find minimum

questions.text:
Each statement gives the constant finite differences of a polynomial function (with $x$-values increasing by 1). For each, state the degree and determine the leading coefficient.

(i) second differences $= {{2*a1}}$ (ii) third differences $= -{{6*a2}}$ (iii) fifth differences $= {{120*a3}}$

parts.label: i
parts.text: Leading coefficient for (i)

parts.label: ii
parts.text: Leading coefficient for (ii)

parts.label: iii
parts.text: Leading coefficient for (iii)

questions.modelAnswer:
(i) Degree 2: $ {{2*a1}} = a \times 2! \Rightarrow a = {{a1}}$.

(ii) Degree 3: $-{{6*a2}} = a \times 3! = 6a \Rightarrow a = -{{a2}}$.

(iii) Degree 5: ${{120*a3}} = a \times 5! = 120a \Rightarrow a = {{a3}}$.

questions.text: Explain the difference between a local maximum point and an absolute maximum point. Then explain why $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$ has a local maximum at $(-1, 2)$ but no absolute maximum.
questions.modelAnswer:
A **local maximum** is higher than all the points *close to it* on either side — a hilltop. An **absolute maximum** is the highest point on the *entire* graph.

For $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$: near $x = -1$, the values are less than $f(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2$ (e.g. $f(-1.5) = 1.125$, $f(-0.5) = 1.375$), so $(-1, 2)$ is a local maximum. But $f$ is a cubic with a positive leading coefficient, so as $x \to \infty$, $f(x) \to \infty$; e.g. $f(3) = 18 > 2$. There is no highest point at all.

rubric.point: Verifies (−1, 2) is higher than nearby points
Uses end behaviour to show no absolute maximum

questions.text:
Without graphing, describe the key features of each function — degree, leading coefficient, end behaviour, $y$-intercept, possible number of $x$-intercepts, maximum number of turning points and whether it has an absolute maximum or minimum.

(i) $g(x) = 0.5x^4 - 3x^2 + 5x$ (ii) $h(x) = x^5 - 7x^3 + 2x - 3$ (iii) $p(x) = -x^6 + 5x^3 + 4$
questions.modelAnswer:
(i) Degree 4, $a = 0.5 > 0$: both ends up (Q2 → Q1). $y$-intercept 0. Between 0 and 4 $x$-intercepts (at least one, since $g(0)=0$). At most 3 turning points. Has an absolute **minimum**, no maximum.

(ii) Degree 5, $a = 1 > 0$: Q3 → Q1. $y$-intercept $-3$. Between 1 and 5 $x$-intercepts. At most 4 turning points. No absolute maximum or minimum.

(iii) Degree 6, $a = -1 < 0$: both ends down (Q3 → Q4). $y$-intercept 4. Between 0 and 6 $x$-intercepts (in fact at least 2, because $p(0) = 4 > 0$ while both ends go to $-\infty$). At most 5 turning points. Has an absolute **maximum**, no minimum.

rubric.point: Reasoning connects features to degree and sign
